question: What is the main goal of a sample design in nursing research?

options.A: To write a budget for a hospital research project
options.B: To plan how to select a portion of the population to study
options.C: To interview hospital managers about staffing levels
options.D: To collect blood samples from patients safely

explanation: Spot on! A sample design is simply your game plan for choosing who will take part in your study so your findings make sense. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h1)

question: Why do nurse researchers study a smaller sample instead of the whole population?

options.A: Hospital ethics committees forbid studying more than ten patients
options.B: It is usually impossible or impractical to study every single person
options.C: Sampling guarantees that zero errors will occur during data collection
options.D: Patients refuse to answer research questions if the group is too large

explanation: You got it! Imagine trying to interview every single diabetic patient in Nigeria—it's way too much work and time. That's why we use a manageable sample. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h1)

question: In research language, what do we mean by the term 'population'?

options.A: The nurses working in a specific hospital ward
options.B: Only the patients who agree to sign the consent form
options.C: The entire group of people the researcher wants to study
options.D: A small group of animals used in laboratory testing

explanation: Correct! The 'population' is the big picture—the complete group of people you are curious about and want your findings to apply to. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h2)

question: What exactly is a sampling frame?

options.A: The statistical formula used to calculate sample size
options.B: The physical list of all eligible members in the target population
options.C: The timeline created for data collection in the ward
options.D: The equipment used to measure vital signs in a study

explanation: Great job! Think of a sampling frame as your actual directory or register (like a ward admission book) from which you pick your participants. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h2)

question: What makes probability sampling special?

options.A: Every member of the population has a known chance of being selected
options.B: The researcher hand-picks individuals who fit a specific profile
options.C: Only patients with severe symptoms are included in the study
options.D: Participants are chosen based on their easy availability to the nurse

explanation: Spot on! Probability sampling uses fairness and random selection, meaning everyone in the group has a fair shot at being chosen. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h3)

question: A researcher decides to pick every 5th patient from the clinic register. Which sampling method is this?
explanation: You nailed it! Going down a list at regular intervals (like every 5th or 10th person) is called systematic sampling. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a non-probability sampling method?
explanation: Correct! Simple random sampling belongs to the probability family because it relies on pure chance, not convenience or choice. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h4)

question: A nurse asks her current study participants to help her connect with other patients who have the same rare condition. What method is this?
explanation: Brilliant! Just like a snowball rolling down a hill and getting bigger, snowball sampling grows as participants introduce you to their friends. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h4)

question: What does 'statistical power' mean in a research study?

options.A: The physical strength required by nurses to lift heavy patients
options.B: The total amount of funding secured for laboratory equipment
options.C: The ability of the study to detect a true effect if one exists
options.D: The speed at which data is entered into a computer spreadsheet

explanation: You got it! Power is basically your study's muscle—its ability to catch a real treatment difference if it's actually there. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h5)

question: What is the big danger of using a sample size that is too small?

options.A: Patients will complain about excessive blood draws and paperwork
options.B: The study may miss important clinical findings and show a false negative
options.C: The hospital ethics committee will automatically ban future studies
options.D: The researchers will spend too much money buying medical supplies

explanation: Spot on! If your sample is too tiny, your study won't have enough muscle to spot a real breakthrough, making it look like nothing happened. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h5)

question: What is sampling bias?

options.A: The deliberate refusal of a patient to answer survey questions
options.B: A systematic flaw where the selection process favors certain outcomes
options.C: An error made by a laboratory technician reading a blood test
options.D: The natural difference between a sample result and the population

explanation: Correct! Sampling bias happens when our selection method accidentally leans too much toward one side, so the sample doesn't truly reflect reality. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h6)

question: How can a nurse researcher best cut down on sampling bias?

options.A: Keep the sample size as small as possible to save time
options.B: Use random selection methods and clear inclusion criteria
options.C: Select only friends and family members who agree to participate
options.D: Ignore patients who do not fit the desired research outcome

explanation: You got it! Randomization and clear rules about who can join keep things fair and help your sample truly represent the wider population. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h6)

question: What makes patient participation in a nursing research study ethical?

options.A: It must be mandatory for all patients admitted to the ward
options.B: It must offer large financial rewards to guarantee compliance
options.C: It must be completely voluntary with informed consent
options.D: It must be approved by senior nursing staff without patient input

explanation: Spot on! Patients must always be fully informed and freely choose to join—no forcing allowed in nursing research! [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h7)

question: Why is patient coercion a serious worry during research recruitment?

options.A: Ethical boards do not allow patients to receive free medication
options.B: Coerced patients always give false answers on questionnaires
options.C: Patients might feel forced to join because their nurse or doctor asked
options.D: Hospital management requires a 100 percent recruitment rate

explanation: Brilliant! Patients respect their nurses and doctors so much that they might fear getting bad care if they say 'no,' which makes true voluntary consent tricky. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T14#GNS217_U3_T14_h7)
